hero.body:
Canadian tourist visits to Florida dropped 13.9 percent in the first half of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025, according to Visit Florida data. The state recorded 1.6 million Canadian tourists through June, while the second quarter alone saw 721,000 Canadian visitors, down 4.2 percent from the second quarter of 2025. Overall, Florida had 73.5 million visitors in the first six months of this year, a decline of 1.4 percent from a year ago.

Business managers in coastal areas say they are seeing the Canadian decline and adapting. Benny Magro, who manages Sandwiches By The Sea on Atlantic Avenue in Delray Beach, said tourism in the area is mostly Canadian and northeastern. "I've been managing businesses in this area for a long time, and we have to adjust," Magro said.

Emily Gasle, a college student studying in Montreal and visiting Delray Beach, attributed some of the sentiment shift to trade policy. "Not trusting, 100 percent," Gasle said. "I feel like because of the tariffs and recent news, obviously there's more of negative feelings." Visit Florida noted that inflation, gas prices and a chilly winter in Florida have had an impact on tourism, but the larger Canadian declines appear to indicate additional factors.

hero.body:
New College of Florida has paid approximately $800,000 to two outside public relations consultants since 2023, both hired through no-bid contracts, even as the school maintains a 13-member in-house marketing and communications team, public records show. The spending comes as Gov. Ron DeSantis has defended more than $60 million in state funding to transform the small liberal arts college of about 1,000 students away from what he calls woke indoctrination.

More than $400,000 has gone to TMF Communications, run by Taryn Fenske, a former spokesperson for both New College President Richard Corcoran during his time as Florida's education commissioner and for Governor DeSantis. Fenske also led DeSantis' presidential super PAC before securing her no-bid contract with New College in July 2023. According to college invoices, Fenske has been paid upwards of $15,000 per month, plus travel expenses, to help improve the school's brand, create proactive messaging, and produce promotional videos. Another nearly $400,000 has gone to Evandr.co, a company run by Katy Saeger, a California PR consultant who describes her crisis communication services as behind the scenes and discreet. Her no-bid contract with New College, signed in November 2023, is worth just over $12,000 per month, plus nearly $30,000 in back pay. This January, Evandr.co's monthly fees were reduced to $5,000.

The consultant spending has raised concerns among faculty members who say they have recently been asked to make budget cuts. New College Professor Sarah Hernandez said she was unaware of the PR spending and questioned the allocation. Last year, a state audit found New College, while the smallest public college in Florida's university system, is also the most financially inefficient. According to the report, it costs nearly three times as much to earn a degree at New College than the University of Florida, the state's largest university. Spending per student at New College during fiscal year 2024 was $83,207, nearly double spending at UF and the highest among all public universities in the state.

New College spokesman Jamie Miller defended the outsourced PR hires, saying the school, like many colleges and universities across Florida, works with outside vendors in a variety of operational areas, including communications and marketing. Miller praised both consultants but did not answer questions about what these consultants have done for the college or why they remain needed since the school has its own 13-member executive communications and marketing team. President Corcoran said the consultants were hired when the school's own PR department wasn't fully staffed and the college was facing state and federal investigations.

New College of Florida has paid approximately $800,000 to two outside public relations consultants since 2023 through no-bid contracts, even as faculty have been asked to make budget cuts and a state audit found the school is the least financially efficient in Florida's university system, public records show. The spending comes despite the school maintaining a 13-member in-house marketing and communications team.

More than $400,000 has gone to TMF Communications, run by Taryn Fenske, a former spokesperson for New College President Richard Corcoran during his time as Florida's education commissioner and for Governor Ron DeSantis. Fenske also led DeSantis' presidential super PAC before securing her no-bid contract with New College in July 2023. According to college invoices, Fenske has been paid upwards of $15,000 per month, plus travel expenses. Another nearly $400,000 has gone to Evandr.co, a company run by Katy Saeger, a California PR consultant whose no-bid contract signed in November 2023 is worth just over $12,000 per month, plus nearly $30,000 in back pay. This January, Evandr.co's monthly fees were reduced to $5,000.

A state audit last year found New College, the smallest public college in Florida's university system, is also the most financially inefficient. According to the report, it costs nearly three times as much to earn a degree at New College than UF, the state's largest university. Spending per student at New College during fiscal year 2024 was $83,207, nearly double spending at UF and the highest among all public universities in the state. New College Professor Sarah Hernandez said she was caught off guard by the spending. "That's a lot of money," Hernandez said. "I was totally unaware of that."

In a statement, New College spokesman Jamie Miller defended the outsourced PR hires, saying the school "like many colleges and universities across Florida, works with outside vendors in a variety of operational areas, including communications and marketing." Miller said the college has been pleased with the consultants' performance but did not answer questions about what they have done or why they remain needed. President Richard Corcoran said the consultants were hired when the school's own PR department wasn't fully staffed and the college was facing state and federal investigations. Ben Wilcox of Integrity Florida, a nonpartisan government watchdog group, said the contracts should raise concerns for taxpayers. "That's pretty much how government operates these days, where we see these kinds of sweetheart deals given to former allies who are being rewarded for their loyalty," Wilcox said.

hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie Police Department said Thursday it received no calls for service involving an active shooter after inaccurate social media posts claimed there was an active shooting near U.S. Highway 1. The activity residents saw was related to a search warrant executed by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office SWAT team at a home on Southeast West Dunbrooke Circle as part of an ongoing criminal investigation.

 Some residents reported hearing gunshots, but law enforcement said the sounds were flash-bang devices used during the operation. The yelling heard in the area was officers giving commands to occupants leaving the home.

 The Port St. Lucie Police Department gave no further details on the criminal investigation officers were responding to. The search warrant execution took place Thursday.

 The false social media posts circulated throughout the day Thursday, prompting the police department to issue a public clarification about the SWAT operation.

cards.body:
The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning for Port St. Lucie on Sunday evening after the EF-0 tornado had already dissipated, leaving residents wondering why the alert came late. The tornado featured very shallow circulation that was not picked up well by radar, according to NWS Melbourne. Reports of the funnel cloud prompted the warning for the tornado that became a waterspout at a point.

Will Ulrich, a meteorologist with NWS Melbourne, said the tornado was on the ground for 10 to 15 minutes, which is not typical during summer months. The brief and weak tornado had winds of 60 to 70 mph. Ulrich said it was one of the typical summer afternoon thunderstorms that generated the tornado.

The National Weather Service issues a tornado warning once it is able to detect a tornado. NWS Melbourne advises residents to have multiple ways to receive warnings to keep themselves and their loved ones safe.

cards.teaser: The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning for Port St. Lucie on Sunday evening after the EF-0 tornado had already dissipated. The shallow circulation of the brief twister prevented radar from detecting it.

The Fort Pierce City Commission decided not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract. At the same time, Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman resigned and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin is set to leave at the end of the month, leaving the city searching for new legal leadership.

Commissioner Michael Broderick said the departures come as Fort Pierce faces several significant development decisions. Broderick pointed specifically to future development proposals on South Hutchinson Island. Among the issues he expects to surface are potential changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density. Broderick said removing those restrictions could clear the way for much taller development on the island.

The commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Rene Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney. The agreement authorizes up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process. Wallace previously worked in the City Attorney's Office before becoming deputy city manager.

cards.teaser: Fort Pierce commissioners voted 3-2 to appoint Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while the city searches for a permanent replacement. The transition comes as the city faces several high-profile development issues expected to come before the City Commission.

Fort Pierce is searching for new legal leadership after the City Commission decided not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract while Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman resigned and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin is set to leave at the end of the month. Commissioner Michael Broderick told CBS12 News the departures come as the city faces several significant development decisions, particularly future proposals on South Hutchinson Island that could include changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density. Broderick said removing those restrictions could clear the way for much taller development on the island.

Commissioners voted 3-2 this week to appoint Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while a search is conducted for a permanent replacement. Broderick voted against the appointment and said the city has no independent legal representation to deal with volatile projects expected to come before the commission. He said appointing the assistant city manager to serve as a charter officer in Fort Pierce creates a conflict with multiple bosses to report to.

Supporters of Wallace's appointment said her previous experience in the City Attorney's Office before becoming deputy city manager positions her to maintain continuity as the city loses much of its legal staff. The commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Renée Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney, authorizing up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process.

A 6-year-old corgi named Luna has been reunited with her owner, Molly Wing-Berman, after going missing when an EF0 tornado struck the Bay St. Lucie community in Port St. Lucie. The tornado pushed open Wing-Berman's locked front door, made a large hole in the wall, swept mail and other items through the locked back door, and deposited them in the pool.

Wing-Berman had taken her 2-year-old rescue dog, Enzo, to the laundry room for safety as the tornado approached, but Luna did not respond or follow. Wing-Berman thought Luna was hiding under the bed in her usual spot. Wing-Berman and her daughter searched the house and yard after the storm. Neighbors eventually found Luna three streets away.

Luna was shaking when found and has stayed close to Wing-Berman since the reunion. Wing-Berman said Luna has been sleeping very close to her. Luna now has a new nickname: Luna ToTo.

PSLPD said it received no calls for service involving an active shooter and dispelled the inaccurate social media posts circulating through the community.

The SWAT operation was part of an ongoing criminal investigation. Some residents reported hearing what they believed were gunshots, but law enforcement said the sounds were flash-bang devices used during the operation.

Yelling heard in the area was officers giving commands to occupants leaving the home. The Port St. Lucie Police Department received calls from concerned residents who had seen the police activity and heard the sounds.

The Port St. Lucie Police Department gave no further details on the criminal investigation officers were responding to.

A grand jury has indicted a Colorado man accused of attempting to shoot and kill five deputy U.S. Marshals during a March 2 confrontation in Vero Beach. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida announced the indictment Thursday.

 Thomas Earl Steffens, 72, was wanted on an arrest warrant in Colorado when he traveled by bus to Vero Beach. A U.S. Marshals fugitive task force tracked him to the city. As law enforcement officers tried to arrest him at the intersection of 12th Street and Commerce Avenue, Steffens opened fire, striking one deputy in the chest and leg. Deputies returned fire, wounding Steffens before taking him into custody.

 Three Indian River County deputies, one Martin County deputy and a deputy U.S. marshal were involved in the incident. A witness said Steffens, who was wanted in Colorado on sexual assault and strangulation charges, fell out of his vehicle with blood on his face as deputies moved in to make the arrest.

 Steffens now faces five counts of attempted murder of a federal officer, one count of aggravated assault of a federal officer and one count of discharging a firearm during a crime of violence. If convicted, he faces up to life in prison.
